hint1: Back when mammoths still roamed, my ancestors grazed steppe stretching from the Carpathians clear across to Beringia—my commute has shrunk a bit since then.
hint2: Nowadays my particular herd sticks to one corner of the map, long gone from places like Ukraine, Moldova, and China.
hint3: I'm the western Mongolia-only branch of a steppe grazer—found nowhere else on the planet, not even elsewhere in Mongolia.
funFacts: During the Pleistocene, this species' range stretched incredibly far, from the British Isles all the way to Beringia. Today one subspecies survives only in a sliver of western Mongolia, having vanished entirely from Romania, Ukraine, Moldova, China, and the rest of Mongolia.

hint1: I'm smaller than a loaf of bread, and I spend my days buried under desert sand where nobody thinks to look.

hint3: I'm the tiniest member of my armor-plated clan, first written up by a scientist back in 1825, and my only living cousin is, well, a bit greater than me.
funFacts: Despite its tough shell, this creature is astonishingly small — adults typically measure under 5 inches long and weigh about as much as a bar of soap. It has only one living relative in its entire subfamily, the greater version of itself.

hint2: My closest living relative is a squat, hammer-crested wader — not the storks I get mistaken for.
hint3: My enormous, boat-shaped beak looks borrowed from a giant's kitchen drawer, and I wade quietly through African swamps hunting for fish.
funFacts: Despite its stork-like looks, genetic evidence places this bird with pelicans and herons, and its nearest relative is actually the hamerkop. Adults are grey, but the young start out brown, and the species is found only in tropical African swamps from South Sudan down to Zambia.

hint3: My forehead sprouts a second, stubby pair of horns in front of my main set — a bovid oddity if ever there was one.
funFacts: This is the only antelope in the world with four horns instead of two, and the front pair can be so tiny they're just fur-covered nubs rather than true horns. The rear horns are always the longer of the two sets, reaching up to about 12 cm.

hint1: I'm one of only four egg-laying mammal cousins left on Earth—yes, we lay eggs and still call ourselves mammals, deal with it.
hint2: My snout goes on for days, and biologists were so charmed by my nose that they built an entire genus name around species like me.
hint3: I roam the forests of a big tropical island north of Australia, sporting the most exaggeratedly elongated snout of my egg-laying relatives—basically the original model for my whole group.
funFacts: This animal was originally classified under a different scientific name, Tachyglossus bruijnii, before being recognized as so distinct it became the namesake type species for its own genus, Zaglossus. It shares its island home with two other Zaglossus species, making it one of three closely related long-snouted egg-layers found there.

hint3: My head has zero hair and my face goes shockingly crimson — like I've been caught blushing forever.

hint3: I'm the one and only living species in my genus, family, and order, native to the Amazon and Orinoco basins.
